Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates — types, digestion, absorption, blood glucose regulation and diabetes.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Classify carbohydrates and name examples of each
  • Describe carbohydrate digestion and absorption
  • Explain how blood glucose is regulated

In simple words

Carbohydrates are the body’s main source of energy. They are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and are broken down into glucose, which cells use for fuel.

Carbohydrates come in three sizes: monosaccharides (single sugar), disaccharides (two sugars) and polysaccharides (many sugars). Most dietary carbohydrate is digested to glucose and absorbed into the blood.

Types of carbohydrates

Type Examples Main feature
Monosaccharides Glucose, fructose, galactose Single sugar units; simplest form
Disaccharides Sucrose, lactose, maltose Two sugar units joined together
Polysaccharides Starch, glycogen, cellulose Many sugar units; storage or fibre

Common food sources:

  • Starch: rice, wheat, potatoes, bread
  • Sugar: table sugar, jaggery, honey, fruits
  • Fibre: whole grains, vegetables, fruits

Digestion and absorption

Carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth with salivary amylase and continues in the small intestine with pancreatic amylase. Brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase) split disaccharides into monosaccharides.

Glucose, galactose and fructose are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into the blood capillaries and travel to the liver through the portal vein.

Blood glucose regulation

  • Insulin (pancreas) lowers blood glucose by moving it into cells and storing it as glycogen.
  • Glucagon (pancreas) raises blood glucose by making the liver break down glycogen.
  • Normal fasting blood glucose: 70–110 mg/dL.
  • Persistently high blood glucose = diabetes mellitus.

🔴 Normal fasting blood glucose

Normal fasting blood glucose is 70–110 mg/dL. Persistently high levels indicate diabetes mellitus.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Diabetic diet — explain meal timing and carbohydrate consistency; refer to dietetics.
  • Blood glucose monitoring — check as ordered, recognize hypoglycaemia (sweating, tremor, confusion).
  • IV fluids — know which solutions contain glucose; never add drugs to blood.
  • Patient teaching — teach signs of high and low blood glucose and when to seek help.
  • Fasting before tests — ensure the patient stays nil by mouth when a fasting glucose is ordered.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Carbohydrates are the body’s main energy source; glucose is the key fuel.
  2. Types: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides.
  3. Digestion: salivary and pancreatic amylase; brush-border enzymes split disaccharides.
  4. Glucose is absorbed through villi into blood and goes to the liver via the portal vein.
  5. Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.
  6. Normal fasting blood glucose: 70–110 mg/dL.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Starch is found in rice, wheat, potatoes and bread.
  2. Lactase digests lactose; lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea.
  3. Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in liver and muscle.
  4. Fibre is not digested but helps bowel movement.

📌 Memory trick

Carbohydrate sizes: “Mono-Di-Poly” — one, two, many sugar units.

60-second revision

  • Carbohydrates = main energy source; glucose = key fuel.
  • Mono-, di-, polysaccharides.
  • Digestion: amylase → brush-border enzymes → monosaccharides.
  • Absorbed via villi to liver.
  • Insulin lowers glucose; glucagon raises it.
  • Fasting glucose: 70–110 mg/dL.

Test yourself

Which is a monosaccharide?

Answer: C. Glucose is a single sugar unit (monosaccharide). Sucrose and lactose are disaccharides; starch is a polysaccharide.

Carbohydrate digestion begins in the:

Answer: B. Salivary amylase in the mouth begins starch digestion.

Normal fasting blood glucose is:

Answer: B. Normal fasting blood glucose is 70–110 mg/dL.

Which hormone lowers blood glucose?

Answer: C. Insulin moves glucose into cells and lowers blood glucose.

Glucose is absorbed into the blood through the:

Answer: B. Monosaccharides are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into blood capillaries.
